subject: Cloud Computing
title: EC2: The Service That Started It All
description: A fast breakdown of EC2: The Service That Started It All for builders.

hook.text: In 2006, AWS launched EC2 and let anyone rent a virtual server for 10 cents an hour.

buildup.text: EC2 offered dozens of instance types: tiny for testing, massive for databases, GPU for machine learning.

discovery.text: You choose your operating system, configure networking, and launch — a full server in under a minute.

twist.text: EC2 instances are ephemeral by default. If the hardware fails, your instance vanishes unless you prepared.

climax.text: Despite being nearly 20 years old, EC2 remains the single largest revenue source for AWS.

punchline.text: EC2 proved that renting servers could build an empire.

quiz.question: What is a key risk of using EC2 instances without proper preparation?
options: Instances can vanish if the underlying hardware fails
EC2 can only run Windows operating systems
Each instance is limited to exactly one hour of runtime

details.summary: Amazon EC2, launched in 2006, was the first major public IaaS offering and remains the backbone of AWS. It lets users launch virtual servers in minutes with configurable CPU, memory, and storage, and its pay-per-second pricing model transformed the industry.
details.whyItMatters: EC2 proved that computing could be consumed as a utility. Understanding its origins explains why AWS dominates cloud computing and how IaaS pricing models work.
takeaways: EC2 launched in 2006 as the first major public IaaS
It offers dozens of instance types for different workloads
Pay-per-second pricing replaced capital hardware purchases

faq.question: How many EC2 instance types exist?
faq.answer: AWS offers over 700 instance types optimized for different workloads: general purpose, compute-optimized, memory-optimized, storage-optimized, and accelerated computing with GPUs. Each type comes in multiple sizes, from tiny to massive.

faq.question: Why did EC2 succeed?
faq.answer: EC2 eliminated the need to buy and rack servers, reduced provisioning from weeks to minutes, and charged only for what was used. Startups could launch with no upfront infrastructure investment, and enterprises could scale without capacity planning cycles.
